clue.text: Interfere with nature poison being brewed

indicators.note: being brewed means the two words nature and poison are stirred together into a fresh mixture

explanation.surface: Someone tampers with the natural world while a toxic concoction bubbles away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being brewed' mixes up the twelve letters of NATURE and POISON; 'with' is a link joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for meddling, butting into other people's affairs uninvited.

clue.text: Discreet puritan not deprived of love'

parts.note: a prude is a person excessively concerned with propriety, a puritan

indicators.note: deprived of means the word not loses the letter that love stands for

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A strait-laced person who still enjoys romance keeps things quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deprived of' takes O away from NOT; love is O because a nil score in tennis looks like the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Being wise and careful in what one says or does is the sense shared by both words.

clue.text: Eager to be second among quite a number

indicators.note: among says the letter for second sits inside the larger number

parts.note: thirty is a fairly large number, taken here as one specific figure

explanation.surface: Someone is keen to come runner-up in a large field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' puts S inside THIRTY; 'quite a number' is vague, but the setter pins it to one figure. 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Craving or keen for something, as in hungry for knowledge, is the figurative sense.

clue.text: The margin 'of error in a dream

indicators.note: of error suggests the letters of the phrase are in a mistaken order and need putting right

explanation.surface: Statistical tolerance features in someone's sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'margin of error' is a statistics phrase, but 'of error' is the anagram signal for THE MARGIN; 'in a' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A frightening, distressing vision during sleep is one kind of dream.

clue.text: Start a fight

definitions.meaning: to begin work on something energetically
a brief quarrel or bout of fisticuffs

explanation.definitionFit: To begin vigorously on a task is the verb sense; a brief scrap or bout is the hyphenated noun.

clue.text: State offers a place 'to work to a scholar

parts.note: a lab, short for laboratory, is a place where scientists work
MA, Master of Arts, is a degree held by a scholar

explanation.surface: A country offers employment to an academic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offers' and the second 'to' are links; MA (Master of Arts) standing for a scholar is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the fifty US states, in the Deep South, with Montgomery as its capital.

clue.text: Hinted the brat was not truthful

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child, a brat
lied means told untruths

explanation.surface: Someone suggested that the naughty child had been lying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' is a link joining definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To suggest something without saying it outright is to hint at it.

clue.text: Bureaucrat to give up post

parts.note: to jack in is British slang for abandoning or quitting
a post is a position or office held

explanation.surface: An official is told to resign from their job.
explanation.walkthrough: JACK IN is informal British for quit; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-important petty official, puffed up by minor authority, is this kind of pen-pusher.

clue.text: A consideration that's funny

parts.note: musing is thoughtful reflection, consideration

explanation.surface: A thought strikes someone as comical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that entertains or causes laughter is funny.

clue.text: Walked about a mile, to go back

indicators.note: back says the assembled letters are read in the opposite direction
about says the word for leaving goes around the mile

parts.note: to depart is to go away
m is the abbreviation for mile

explanation.surface: Someone strolled about a mile before turning round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts M inside DEPART to make DEPMART, which 'back' turns round. 'go back' looks like one phrase, but 'to go' is DEPART.
explanation.definitionFit: To trudge or trek a long way on foot is a heavy kind of walking.

clue.text: Auxiliary machinery needing no key to work

indicators.note: to work means the letters of the phrase are set to work in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A backup engine runs without needing a key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to work' rearranges NEEDING NO KEY.
explanation.definitionFit: A small auxiliary steam engine, used for hoisting or pumping on ships, goes by this name.

clue.text: Parliament plunged into darkness eternally

indicators.note: plunged into suggests the answer is sunk within the run of the following words

explanation.surface: A legislature has been cast into permanent gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the Israeli parliament, sitting inside darKNESS ETernally.
explanation.definitionFit: Israel's single-chamber national legislature in Jerusalem.

clue.text: Talk of poetic measure

parts.note: o' is the poetic or dialect contraction of of, as in will-o'-the-wisp
a ration is a fixed measured allowance

explanation.surface: A discussion of verse metre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poetic measure' looks like metre, but 'poetic' tells you to shorten 'of' to its literary form O'.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal speech, as at a ceremony, is a kind of talk.

clue.text: Bats like pecans

definitions.meaning: pecans are hard-shelled tree kernels, so this means tasting of or full of kernels

explanation.definitionFit: Crazy is one sense, slang shared with bats; full of kernels, as pecans are, is the other.

clue.text: At first they rode in a seat, not side-saddle

indicators.note: in places the two initials inside the phrase for a seat

parts.note: a saddle is the seat on a horse or bicycle

indicators.note: At first takes the opening letter of each of the next two words

explanation.surface: Early riders sat with legs on either side of the horse rather than side-saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' takes the initials of 'they rode'; 'in' sets them just after the S of the seat phrase. The definition is the riding style opposed to side-saddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitting with legs either side, astride, is the opposite of riding with both legs on one side.

clue.text: Make smaller viewer

definitions.meaning: to shorten by sliding sections into one another
an optical instrument for seeing distant objects

explanation.definitionFit: Collapsing sections into each other shortens a thing; the optical tube for seeing far is the noun.

clue.text: Where to move in to explore coast

indicators.note: in says those shifted letters go inside the word for explore

parts.note: to feel is to explore by touch

indicators.note: to move asks for the letters of where to be shifted about

explanation.surface: Somewhere to relocate so one can investigate the seashore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coast' looks like the seashore but is a verb, to roll without power; 'to move' scrambles 'Where' and 'in' slips the result after the first letter of the touch word.
explanation.definitionFit: To roll along without pedalling or engine power is to coast.

clue.text: Every other one seen using a cruel trap

indicators.note: Every other one picks alternate letters, starting with the second, from the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: Alternate individuals are observed setting a vicious snare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every other one' takes the 2nd, 4th, 6th and so on letters of 'seen using a cruel'.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch in a snare; both words are verbs for capturing.

clue.text: Law they broke with 22

indicators.note: broke says the words law and they are smashed and their letters reassembled

explanation.surface: They broke the law for gain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with 22' sends you to 22 down, money; being with money is being rich. 'broke' looks like penniless but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Having plenty of cash means being rich.

clue.text: Class shown by actors when speaking

indicators.note: when speaking means the word for actors is heard rather than read

parts.note: the cast is the set of actors in a play

explanation.surface: Social standing is betrayed by performers' accents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shown by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A hereditary social rank, as in the traditional Hindu system, is a class.

clue.text: Set small building above the, lake

indicators.note: above in a down clue puts the first piece over the second

parts.note: a cot is an old word for a small cottage or shelter
Erie is one of the North American Great Lakes

explanation.surface: A little hut perches above the lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' is a link; in a down answer 'above' means placed before.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclusive circle or clique of like-minded people is a set.

clue.text: Sort of milk Frenchwoman fed to second child

indicators.note: fed to says the Frenchwoman goes into the word for the youngster

parts.note: a kid is a child
Mme is the abbreviation for Madame, a French married woman

explanation.surface: A French nanny gives low-fat milk to the younger child.
explanation.walkthrough: Mme is the usual written short form of Madame; 'fed to' puts her inside the second-plus-child pair, after the K.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk with the cream taken off the top is described this way.

clue.text: This month everybody is put in place

parts.note: inst., short for instant, is old business jargon for this month
all means everybody

explanation.surface: This month, everyone gets settled into their positions.
explanation.walkthrough: INST (instant) was used in old commercial letters for the current month; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To fit or set up, as with equipment or an official in a post.

clue.text: Money Poirot put up? Not he!

indicators.note: put up in a down clue means the letters are read upward, in reverse
Not he tells us to take away the letters of he from the detective's first name

parts.note: Hercule Poirot is Agatha Christie's Belgian detective

explanation.surface: Did Poirot put up the cash? Certainly not!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' removes H and E from HERCULE, leaving ERCUL, which 'put up' reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: A derogatory word for cash, especially ill-gotten gains.

clue.text: The environment is going down

definitions.meaning: surroundings, the backdrop in which something happens
sinking below the horizon, as the sun does at dusk

explanation.surface: The world's ecology is in decline.
explanation.definitionFit: Surroundings or backdrop is one sense; sinking below the horizon, like the sun, is the other.

clue.text: Adaptable call girl held back

indicators.note: back says the whole construction is read in reverse
held means one word grips the girl's name inside it

parts.note: to cite is to summon or call, as before a court
Sal is a girl's name, short for Sally

explanation.surface: A versatile escort was detained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'call girl' looks like one phrase but splits in two. 'held' puts the girl inside the call word, giving CITSALE, which 'back' reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: Able to stretch and return to shape, hence flexible.

clue.text: Crew — one possibly including a warrant officer

indicators.note: including says the rearranged word wraps around the other pieces
possibly signals a variant arrangement of the letters of one

parts.note: RSM, regimental sergeant major, is a warrant officer rank in the British Army

explanation.surface: A team in which one member might be a senior army NCO.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges the word as OEN, and 'including' wraps it round the rest; the regimental sergeant major is a warrant officer class one in the British Army.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowers making up a boat's team form a crew.

clue.text: Round each turning tear like a dean

indicators.note: turning says each of the two words before it is flipped round in place

parts.note: a rev is one revolution or round of an engine
every means each
to rend is to tear

explanation.surface: Each time the dean spins round, a rip appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' flips each of the first two words in place, giving VER and YREVE. The Very Reverend is the formal style of a Church of England dean.
explanation.definitionFit: Church of England deans are formally addressed by this honorific style.
